title: Yes Bank and RBI Ask Supreme Court to Review Verdict Restoring Rs 8,415 Crore of AT1 Bonds
excerpt: Both the bank and the regulator filed review petitions on November 13 against the October 15 judgment that quashed the 2020 AT1 write-down, while bondholders pursue contempt proceedings to force restoration.
body:
• Yes Bank and the Reserve Bank of India have filed review petitions asking the Supreme Court to reconsider its October 15 judgment that quashed the write-down of Rs 8,415 crore of Yes Bank AT1 bonds.
  • The court had upheld the Bombay High Court's 2023 ruling that the bank's administrator acted beyond his authority: the write-down came on March 14, 2020, a day after the final reconstruction scheme took force, and the scheme no longer authorised it.
  • Yes Bank confirmed its petition in a November 13 stock exchange disclosure that did not detail its grounds; the RBI's petition was also filed on November 13, according to the Supreme Court website.
  • Bondholders are not waiting: Axis Trustee, acting for them, e-filed contempt proceedings on November 6, alleging the bank has offered no concrete roadmap to restore the bonds.

Yes Bank and the Reserve Bank of India have asked the Supreme Court to review its October 15 judgment restoring Rs 8,415 crore of the bank's additional tier-1 (AT1) bonds, reopening a five-year legal fight over losses imposed on bondholders during the bank's 2020 rescue. Bar and Bench reported the filings on Monday, and Business Standard reported that the RBI's review petition was filed on November 13, per the Supreme Court website. Yes Bank had confirmed its own petition in a stock exchange disclosure dated November 13, which did not set out its grounds.

What the court decided in October

"The court held that the bank's administrator could not have assumed the RBI's regulatory powers to write down the bonds, and that his authority did not continue through the reconstruction process."

A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih on October 15 dismissed the appeals filed by Yes Bank, the RBI and the Union government, and upheld the Bombay High Court's January 20, 2023 judgment setting aside the write-down. The court held that the bank's administrator could not have assumed the RBI's regulatory powers to write down the bonds, and that his authority did not continue through the reconstruction process.

The sequence mattered. The RBI's reconstruction scheme for Yes Bank, drawn up under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 after the lender's finances deteriorated, came into force in its final form on March 13, 2020 - and the government had removed from the approved scheme the provision expressly authorising a write-down. The administrator announced the write-down of the outstanding AT1 bonds on March 14, 2020, one day too late, the courts held. The Supreme Court also held that annual coupons on the bonds would remain unaffected and must be paid in line with the bonds' information memorandums.

The bonds at stake

The dispute covers two issuances: Rs 3,000 crore of AT1 bonds carrying a 9.5% coupon, issued in December 2016, and Rs 5,415 crore carrying a 9%, issued in October 2017. AT1 bonds are bank debt designed to absorb losses when a lender runs into trouble - which is what made their treatment in the Yes Bank rescue a precedent-setting fight. Axis Trustee Services, acting for the debenture holders alongside individual bondholders and other investors, first challenged the write-down in the Bombay High Court in May 2020.

What is at stake now

Reinstating the principal could cut Yes Bank's common equity tier-1 (CET1) capital ratio by around 250 basis points, based on the bank's June 2026 position, Business Standard reported, though it would not affect the tier-1 ratio in the same way. The review petitions, filed under Article 137 of the Constitution, are a narrow remedy - a review asks the same court to correct an error apparent on the face of the record - and neither report gave a hearing date.

Bondholders, meanwhile, are pressing for execution rather than argument. After the October judgment, Axis Trustee sought restoration of the bonds and their associated rights, including in depository and exchange records, and on November 6 it e-filed contempt proceedings against Yes Bank and certain officials and directors, alleging the bank had failed to provide a concrete roadmap for compliance.
